title: Weights & Measures — Speculative Decoding and the Same-Model Question
description: Fast Inference from Transformers via Speculative Decoding — Leviathan, Kalman, Matias (Google Research, 2022; ICML 2023); with Accelerating Large Language Model Decoding with Speculative Sampling — Chen, Borgeaud, Irving et al. (DeepMind, 2023)
show_notes:
Fast Inference from Transformers via Speculative Decoding — Leviathan, Kalman, Matias (Google Research, 2022; ICML 2023); with Accelerating Large Language Model Decoding with Speculative Sampling — Chen, Borgeaud, Irving et al. (DeepMind, 2023)

A large language model spends most of each step reading its own weights from memory, so its arithmetic sits idle. Jack and Molly unpack speculative decoding (Leviathan, Kalman and Matias at Google Research, first posted November 2022, ICML 2023; found independently by DeepMind's Chen and colleagues, posted February 2023): a small model drafts several words, the big model checks them all in one pass, and a weighted keep-or-replace rule makes the output distribution exactly the big model's own, so a weak drafter costs speed, not quality. Then what the papers measured (about two to three times faster, one request at a time), the drafters built onto the model since (Medusa, EAGLE, DeepSeek's multi-token prediction, Google's Gemma 4 drafters), why busy servers shrink the gain, and the policy question: what should count as the same model when the serving layer underneath it can change.

Notes: the headline speedups are batch-of-one results on Google's TPU chips; under heavy traffic one open-source serving engine measured slowdowns instead. "Exact" means the same distribution in exact arithmetic: DeepMind's paper says identical outputs can't be expected on real hardware, and relaxed, non-exact checking modes also ship under the speculative decoding label. Greedy guess-and-check decoding predates the paper (Stern and colleagues, 2018), and a Peking University and Microsoft team used the name first, in September 2022. The readings of the EU Code of Practice form, the European Commission's one-third-of-training-compute test and California's SB 53 on air are the hosts' own.

Jack and Molly are AI-generated hosts; research and script by Oggy.
